metadata.title: STOPP-relevant UK medicines dataset
metadata.purpose: Contextual medicine-name matching layer for a static medication review website. This file is intended to support STOPP-relevant prompts during medication review and should not be used as an automatic prescribing rule engine.

primaryReferences.title: STOPP/START criteria for potentially inappropriate prescribing in older people: version 3

notes: Many STOPP criteria depend on duration, indication, renal function, falls history, heart failure, constipation, delirium risk, and other clinical context.
A matched medicine should therefore be displayed as STOPP-relevant with context to review, not as an automatic breach.

entries.criterionSummary: Oxybutynin is contraindicated in dementia or chronic cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); also flagged in recurrent falls (K12), concurrent use of 2+ antimuscarinics (M1), and delirium or dementia (D14).
contextToCheck: Total anticholinergic burden (M1 — count of concurrent antimuscarinics)
entries.whyItMatters: Oxybutynin has high CNS penetration and is the most cognitively hazardous antimuscarinic OAB agent in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with high post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and polyanticholinergic regimens (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Anticholinergic burden from OAB agents contributes to confusion, urinary retention, constipation and falls in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); also flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and concurrent antimuscarinic use (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Adds to anticholinergic burden and may precipitate or worsen urinary retention, confusion and falls.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and polyanticholinergic regimens (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Contributes to anticholinergic burden despite lower CNS penetration than oxybutynin.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); also flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and concurrent antimuscarinic use (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Selective M3 antagonism does not eliminate risk of cognitive and urinary adverse effects in frail older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and polyanticholinergic regimens (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Contributes to anticholinergic burden and falls risk; often interchangeable concerns apply to all agents in this class.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and concurrent antimuscarinic use (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Mixed calcium-channel and antimuscarinic action still carries the class-wide anticholinergic safety concerns.

entries.criterionSummary: Antimuscarinic for overactive bladder contraindicated in dementia or cognitive impairment (I1), narrow-angle glaucoma (I2), BPH with post-void residual >200 ml (I3), and chronic constipation (I4); flagged in recurrent falls (K12) and polyanticholinergic regimens (M1).
entries.whyItMatters: Limited efficacy data combined with full anticholinergic safety risks makes this agent particularly problematic in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Procyclidine used to treat antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal symptoms is rarely justified and risks cognitive worsening (D13); contraindicated in delirium or dementia (D14).
contextToCheck: Indication — is it solely for antipsychotic-induced EPS?
Whether the causative antipsychotic can be reduced or switched
entries.whyItMatters: Procyclidine adds substantial anticholinergic burden and should rarely be used in older adults, particularly those with cognitive impairment.

entries.criterionSummary: Used to treat antipsychotic-induced EPS, this is rarely justified and risks cognitive worsening (D13); contraindicated in delirium or dementia (D14).
contextToCheck: Indication — is it solely for antipsychotic-induced EPS?
Whether the causative antipsychotic can be reduced or switched
entries.whyItMatters: One of the highest-burden anticholinergic agents; especially hazardous in dementia and delirium.

entries.criterionSummary: Used to treat antipsychotic-induced EPS, this is rarely justified and risks cognitive worsening (D13); contraindicated in delirium or dementia (D14).
contextToCheck: Indication — is it solely for antipsychotic-induced EPS?
Whether the causative antipsychotic can be reduced or switched
entries.whyItMatters: High anticholinergic burden; use in older adults with cognitive impairment is strongly discouraged.

entries.criterionSummary: Used to treat antipsychotic-induced EPS, this is rarely justified and risks cognitive worsening (D13); contraindicated in delirium or dementia (D14).
contextToCheck: Indication — is it solely for antipsychotic-induced EPS?
Whether the causative antipsychotic can be reduced or switched
entries.whyItMatters: Anticholinergic agent with risk of worsening cognition, delirium and urinary retention in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Chlorpromazine carries high antimuscarinic burden and is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH (D4), delirium or dementia (D14), BPSD use beyond 12 weeks without review (D15), and as a first-line agent for psychosis or BPSD given its sedative and EPS profile (D21); also a falls risk (K2).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH
entries.whyItMatters: High anticholinergic and sedative load makes chlorpromazine particularly unsuitable in older adults with cognitive impairment or falls risk.

entries.criterionSummary: Clozapine has very high antimuscarinic burden and is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH with urinary retention risk (D4) and in delirium or dementia (D14).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or urinary retention history
entries.whyItMatters: Clozapine's extreme anticholinergic burden can cause urinary retention, severe constipation and delirium, and its use in older adults with dementia requires specialist justification.

entries.criterionSummary: Flupentixol is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH (D4), delirium or dementia (D14), BPSD use beyond 12 weeks without review (D15), and contributes to falls risk (K2).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH
entries.whyItMatters: Anticholinergic and EPS profile of flupentixol adds to risk of retention, falls and worsened cognition in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Fluphenazine carries anticholinergic burden and is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH (D4), delirium or dementia (D14), BPSD use beyond 12 weeks without review (D15), as a first-line BPSD agent given its EPS profile (D21), and as a falls risk (K2).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH
Depot formulation — frequency and indication review
entries.whyItMatters: High EPS and anticholinergic burden make fluphenazine especially problematic in frail older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Promazine carries significant anticholinergic and sedative burden and is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH (D4), delirium or dementia (D14), BPSD use beyond 12 weeks without review (D15), as a first-line phenothiazine for psychosis or BPSD (D21), and as a falls risk (K2).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH
entries.whyItMatters: Promazine's combination of sedation, anticholinergic and orthostatic effects carries a high adverse-event burden in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Aripiprazole used for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia should be reviewed after 12 weeks unless symptoms remain severe and non-pharmacological alternatives have been tried (D5/D15); also contributes to falls risk (K2).
entries.whyItMatters: Even atypical antipsychotics with lower anticholinergic burden carry cerebrovascular and falls risk in older adults with dementia.

entries.criterionSummary: Donepezil is contraindicated with resting bradycardia <60 bpm, heart block, or recurrent syncope (D17) and should be reviewed when combined with beta-blockers, digoxin, diltiazem or verapamil due to additive bradycardia risk (D18).
contextToCheck: ECG — PR interval and heart block
Concurrent bradycardic drugs (beta-blockers, digoxin, diltiazem, verapamil)
entries.whyItMatters: AChE inhibitors reduce heart rate; combination with other bradycardic agents substantially increases syncope and heart block risk.

entries.criterionSummary: Rivastigmine is contraindicated with resting bradycardia <60 bpm, heart block, or recurrent syncope (D17) and should be reviewed when combined with beta-blockers, digoxin, diltiazem or verapamil due to additive bradycardia risk (D18).
contextToCheck: ECG — PR interval and heart block
entries.whyItMatters: Bradycardic risk is a class effect; patch formulation does not eliminate cardiac concern.

entries.criterionSummary: Galantamine is contraindicated with resting bradycardia <60 bpm, heart block, or recurrent syncope (D17) and should be reviewed when combined with beta-blockers, digoxin, diltiazem or verapamil due to additive bradycardia risk (D18).
contextToCheck: ECG — PR interval and heart block
entries.whyItMatters: Additive bradycardia risk with other rate-limiting drugs can precipitate syncope and falls.

entries.criterionSummary: Memantine should be reviewed in patients with a history of seizure disorder, as NMDA antagonism may lower the seizure threshold (D19).
contextToCheck: Renal function — dose adjustment required if eGFR <30
entries.whyItMatters: Use in patients with active or recent seizure history may increase seizure risk and requires specialist review.

entries.criterionSummary: Prochlorperazine worsens extrapyramidal symptoms in Parkinsonism (F1) and as a phenothiazine it is flagged as a first-line agent for psychosis or BPSD given its sedative and EPS profile (D21).
contextToCheck: Indication — is there an alternative anti-emetic (e.g. domperidone, ondansetron)?
entries.whyItMatters: Can markedly worsen motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease and is a frequent contributor to drug-induced Parkinsonism.

entries.criterionSummary: Metoclopramide worsens extrapyramidal symptoms in patients with Parkinsonism and should be avoided in this group; alternatives should be used for nausea and vomiting (F1).
contextToCheck: Indication — is there a non-dopamine-blocking alternative?
entries.whyItMatters: Central dopamine blockade precipitates or worsens Parkinsonism, sometimes irreversibly.

entries.criterionSummary: Mirabegron should be avoided in labile or severe hypertension (I6) and has QT-prolonging potential requiring review in patients with known QTc prolongation or concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (B15).
contextToCheck: Current blood pressure and antihypertensive regimen
History of labile or severe hypertension
entries.whyItMatters: Can raise blood pressure significantly in poorly controlled hypertension and adds to QT prolongation risk.

entries.criterionSummary: Gabapentin used for non-neuropathic pain has no proven benefit and carries sedation, falls and misuse risk (L5); as an anti-epileptic it is also flagged in recurrent falls due to sedation and ataxia (K5).
contextToCheck: Indication — is there confirmed neuropathic pain?
Renal function (dose reduction required if eGFR reduced)
entries.whyItMatters: Gabapentin contributes to sedation, ataxia and falls, and its use for non-neuropathic pain is not evidence-based.

entries.criterionSummary: Pregabalin used for non-neuropathic pain has no proven benefit and carries sedation, falls and misuse risk (L5); as an anti-epileptic it is also flagged in recurrent falls due to sedation and ataxia (K5).
contextToCheck: Indication — is there confirmed neuropathic pain?
entries.whyItMatters: Pregabalin has high misuse potential and significantly adds to sedation and falls risk in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Digoxin is inappropriate in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (B1), in bradycardia <50 bpm or significant heart block (B4), and as first-line therapy for AF rate control beyond 3 months where superior alternatives exist (B21).
contextToCheck: Echocardiogram — is EF preserved or reduced?
Heart rate and ECG (PR interval, heart block)
AF indication — is this first-line rate control?
Renal function (narrow therapeutic index, toxicity if eGFR reduced)
entries.whyItMatters: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and is especially prone to toxicity in older adults with reduced renal function.

entries.criterionSummary: Verapamil is contraindicated in NYHA class III/IV heart failure (B2), in combination with beta-blockers due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia <50 bpm or significant heart block (B4), and increases dabigatran exposure (C13).
contextToCheck: Heart failure class and ejection fraction
Resting heart rate and ECG (PR interval, heart block)
entries.whyItMatters: Verapamil can precipitate acute decompensation in heart failure and life-threatening bradyarrhythmias when combined with beta-blockers.

entries.criterionSummary: Diltiazem is contraindicated in NYHA class III/IV heart failure (B2), in combination with beta-blockers due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia <50 bpm or significant heart block (B4), and increases dabigatran exposure (C13).
contextToCheck: Heart failure class and ejection fraction
Resting heart rate and ECG (PR interval, heart block)
entries.whyItMatters: Combination with beta-blockers is a common prescription error that can cause complete heart block.

entries.criterionSummary: Amiodarone should not be used as first-line treatment for supraventricular tachycardia due to its extensive toxicity profile (B6) and is a potent QT-prolonging agent requiring review in patients with known QTc prolongation (B15).
contextToCheck: Is amiodarone genuinely first-line for SVT?
Thyroid, pulmonary and hepatic function monitoring
entries.whyItMatters: Amiodarone has the highest organ toxicity profile of any antiarrhythmic and requires active surveillance even at maintenance doses.

entries.criterionSummary: Methyldopa is poorly tolerated in older people and should generally be avoided as an antihypertensive (B11); it is also specifically flagged in patients with recurrent falls (K11).
contextToCheck: Whether better-tolerated alternatives have been tried
entries.whyItMatters: Methyldopa causes sedation, depression and postural hypotension that substantially increase falls and confusion risk in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Clonidine is poorly tolerated in older people due to sedation and rebound hypertension risk, and should generally be avoided as an antihypertensive (B11); also flagged in patients with recurrent falls (K11).
contextToCheck: Risk of rebound hypertension on discontinuation
entries.whyItMatters: Sedation, postural hypotension and rebound hypertension on cessation are clinically dangerous in frail older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Moxonidine is poorly tolerated in older people and should generally be avoided as an antihypertensive (B11); it is also flagged in patients with recurrent falls (K11).
contextToCheck: Whether better-tolerated alternatives have been tried
entries.whyItMatters: Central sympatholysis contributes to sedation and postural hypotension with associated falls risk.

entries.criterionSummary: Alfuzosin should be avoided in patients with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or syncope history (I5); as an antihypertensive it is also flagged in recurrent falls (K9) and specifically for prostatic outflow symptoms in recurrent falls (K10).
entries.whyItMatters: First-dose and sustained postural hypotension from alpha-1 blockade is a significant falls risk in older men.

entries.criterionSummary: Doxazosin should be avoided in patients with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or syncope history (I5); as an antihypertensive it is also flagged in recurrent falls (K9) and for prostatic outflow symptoms in recurrent falls (K10).
entries.whyItMatters: Alpha-1 blockade causes postural hypotension; falls risk is amplified when combined with other antihypertensives.

entries.criterionSummary: Tamsulosin should be avoided in patients with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or syncope history (I5) and is flagged for prostatic outflow symptom use in patients with recurrent falls (K10).
contextToCheck: Is this first-line for BPH with safer alternatives available?
entries.whyItMatters: Selective urological alpha-1 blockers still cause postural hypotension, adding materially to falls risk in frail older men.

entries.criterionSummary: Terazosin should be avoided in patients with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or syncope history (I5); as an antihypertensive it is flagged in recurrent falls (K9) and for prostatic outflow symptom use in recurrent falls (K10).
entries.whyItMatters: Persistent postural hypotension makes terazosin a significant falls and syncope risk, especially in frail older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Indoramin should be avoided in patients with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or syncope history (I5); as an antihypertensive it is flagged in recurrent falls (K9) and for prostatic outflow symptom use in recurrent falls (K10).
entries.whyItMatters: Indoramin's additional sedative action increases falls risk beyond simple postural hypotension.

entries.criterionSummary: Tiotropium should be reviewed in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma or bladder outflow obstruction, as inhaled anticholinergic delivery does not fully prevent systemic effects (G3).
entries.whyItMatters: Even inhaled LAMAs can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma or worsen urinary retention in susceptible patients.

entries.criterionSummary: Aclidinium should be reviewed in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma or bladder outflow obstruction, as inhaled anticholinergic delivery does not fully prevent systemic effects (G3).
entries.whyItMatters: Inhaled anticholinergics can worsen glaucoma and urinary retention in susceptible patients.

entries.criterionSummary: Umeclidinium (alone or in combination inhalers) should be reviewed in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma or bladder outflow obstruction (G3).
contextToCheck: Total anticholinergic burden including combination inhaler components
entries.whyItMatters: Combination inhalers containing LAMAs are easy to overlook as anticholinergic contributors in polypharmacy reviews.

entries.criterionSummary: Glycopyrronium (alone or in combination inhalers) should be reviewed in patients with narrow-angle glaucoma or bladder outflow obstruction (G3).
contextToCheck: Total anticholinergic burden including combination inhaler components
entries.whyItMatters: Glycopyrronium in combination inhalers may not be readily identified as an antimuscarinic contributor during medication review.

entries.criterionSummary: Citalopram is flagged in hyponatraemia (Na <130, D6), current or recent significant bleeding (D7), combined with anticoagulants where there is a major haemorrhage history (C12), in recurrent falls (K8), and at doses above 20 mg due to QT prolongation (B15).
contextToCheck: QTc interval — avoid >20 mg/day if QTc prolonged
Dose: UK maximum is 20 mg/day in patients over 65
entries.whyItMatters: Citalopram has the highest QT-prolonging risk among common SSRIs and its UK licensed dose is halved in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Escitalopram is flagged in hyponatraemia (Na <130, D6), current or recent significant bleeding (D7), combined with anticoagulants where there is a major haemorrhage history (C12), in recurrent falls (K8), and at doses above 10 mg due to QT prolongation (B15).
contextToCheck: QTc interval — avoid >10 mg/day in older adults if QTc prolonged
Dose: UK maximum is 10 mg/day in patients over 65
entries.whyItMatters: Escitalopram shares citalopram's QT risk; the maximum licensed dose in older adults is half the general adult dose.

entries.criterionSummary: Sertraline is flagged in hyponatraemia (Na <130, D6), current or recent significant bleeding (D7), combined with anticoagulants where there is a major haemorrhage history (C12), and in recurrent falls (K8).
entries.whyItMatters: Generally preferred SSRI in older adults but still carries hyponatraemia, bleeding augmentation and falls risks.

entries.criterionSummary: Fluoxetine is flagged in hyponatraemia (Na <130, D6), current or recent significant bleeding (D7), combined with anticoagulants where there is a major haemorrhage history (C12), and in recurrent falls (K8).
contextToCheck: Drug interactions — long half-life means interactions persist after stopping
entries.whyItMatters: Fluoxetine's very long half-life prolongs drug interaction risks and makes it harder to manage adverse effects promptly.

entries.criterionSummary: Venlafaxine should be avoided in patients with severe hypertension (SBP >180 mmHg or DBP >105 mmHg) due to noradrenergic-mediated blood pressure elevation (D3).
contextToCheck: Current blood pressure — systolic and diastolic
Blood pressure monitoring at initiation and dose changes
Reason for SNRI selection over SSRI
entries.whyItMatters: Noradrenergic activity can raise blood pressure substantially, particularly at higher doses, creating cardiovascular risk in poorly controlled hypertension.

entries.criterionSummary: Duloxetine should be avoided in severe hypertension (SBP >180 mmHg or DBP >105 mmHg, D3) and in patients with urinary urgency or urge incontinence as it may worsen these symptoms (I7).
contextToCheck: Current blood pressure — systolic and diastolic
Lower urinary tract symptoms — urgency and urge incontinence
Indication — pain, depression, or incontinence treatment?
entries.whyItMatters: Duloxetine can worsen urinary urgency through noradrenergic tone at the bladder neck and simultaneously elevate blood pressure.

entries.criterionSummary: Glibenclamide is a long-acting sulphonylurea in type 2 diabetes that carries a significantly higher risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia than shorter-acting alternatives and should be avoided in older adults (J1).
contextToCheck: Type 2 diabetes — is glibenclamide appropriate given age?
Whether gliclazide or a DPP4-inhibitor would be safer
entries.whyItMatters: Long-acting sulphonylureas cause prolonged hypoglycaemia that may be missed in older adults and can precipitate falls, confusion and cardiac events.

entries.criterionSummary: Glimepiride is a long-acting sulphonylurea in type 2 diabetes carrying hypoglycaemia risk; STOPP recommends preference for shorter-acting agents such as gliclazide in older adults (J1).
contextToCheck: Type 2 diabetes — is a long-acting SU appropriate?
Whether gliclazide or a DPP4-inhibitor would be safer
entries.whyItMatters: Prolonged hypoglycaemia from long-acting sulphonylureas is particularly dangerous in older adults with limited awareness of hypoglycaemic symptoms.

entries.criterionSummary: Gliclazide is the preferred sulphonylurea in older adults in the UK; it is flagged as a class representative under STOPP J1 to prompt review of hypoglycaemia risk and glycaemic targets even with shorter-acting agents.
contextToCheck: HbA1c target — is 48–53 mmol/mol appropriate for this patient?
Whether dose reduction or a DPP4-inhibitor would be safer
entries.whyItMatters: Even gliclazide can cause clinically significant hypoglycaemia in older adults with variable dietary intake or renal impairment.

entries.criterionSummary: Pioglitazone is contraindicated in patients with heart failure due to its fluid-retaining properties, which can precipitate acute decompensation (J2).
contextToCheck: Heart failure diagnosis and NYHA class
entries.whyItMatters: Pioglitazone causes sodium and water retention that can rapidly worsen heart failure and should be avoided in all grades of this condition.

entries.criterionSummary: Metformin should be withheld or dose-reduced if eGFR falls below 30 ml/min/1.73 m² due to risk of lactic acidosis accumulation (E6).
entries.whyItMatters: Lactic acidosis from metformin accumulation in severe renal impairment can be life-threatening.

entries.criterionSummary: Canagliflozin should be reviewed in patients with symptomatic hypotension, as SGLT2 inhibitors cause volume depletion that may worsen haemodynamic instability (J4).
contextToCheck: eGFR (efficacy and safety threshold varies by agent)
entries.whyItMatters: Volume depletion from glucosuria can precipitate symptomatic hypotension, especially in older adults on multiple antihypertensive agents.

entries.criterionSummary: Dapagliflozin should be reviewed in patients with symptomatic hypotension, as SGLT2 inhibitors cause volume depletion that may worsen haemodynamic instability (J4).
contextToCheck: eGFR (avoid if eGFR <25 for diabetes indication)
entries.whyItMatters: Volume depletion can precipitate falls and acute kidney injury, particularly in frail older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Empagliflozin should be reviewed in patients with symptomatic hypotension, as SGLT2 inhibitors cause volume depletion that may worsen haemodynamic instability (J4).
contextToCheck: eGFR (avoid if eGFR <30 for diabetes indication)
entries.whyItMatters: Volume-depleting mechanism adds to falls and renal impairment risk in polypharmacy-heavy older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Ertugliflozin should be reviewed in patients with symptomatic hypotension, as SGLT2 inhibitors cause volume depletion that may worsen haemodynamic instability (J4).
contextToCheck: eGFR (avoid if eGFR <45 for diabetes indication)
entries.whyItMatters: Class-wide volume-depleting mechanism creates risk of symptomatic hypotension and falls.

entries.criterionSummary: Phenytoin is flagged in patients with recurrent falls due to sedation, ataxia and cerebellar toxicity risk (K5).
contextToCheck: Drug interactions — phenytoin is a potent inducer
Osteoporosis risk (enzyme induction reduces vitamin D)
entries.whyItMatters: Phenytoin causes cerebellar toxicity and ataxia at supratherapeutic levels, substantially increasing falls risk in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Carbamazepine is flagged in patients with recurrent falls due to sedation, ataxia and hyponatraemia risk (K5).
contextToCheck: Serum sodium — risk of SIADH-related hyponatraemia
entries.whyItMatters: Carbamazepine causes sedation, ataxia and hyponatraemia, all of which independently increase falls risk.

entries.criterionSummary: Sodium valproate is flagged in patients with recurrent falls due to sedation and tremor risk (K5).
entries.whyItMatters: Valproate-induced tremor and sedation can significantly increase falls risk in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Lamotrigine is flagged in patients with recurrent falls due to sedation and dizziness, particularly at higher doses (K5).
contextToCheck: Dizziness or balance problems at current dose
Drug interactions — valproate doubles lamotrigine levels
entries.whyItMatters: Dose-dependent sedation and dizziness from lamotrigine contribute to falls risk, requiring careful dose titration in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Levetiracetam is flagged in patients with recurrent falls due to sedation and behavioural side effects that may increase fall risk (K5).
contextToCheck: Behavioural changes — irritability, agitation (common side effect)
Renal function — dose reduction required if eGFR reduced
entries.whyItMatters: Behavioural and sedative adverse effects of levetiracetam can increase falls risk; renal dose adjustment is commonly required.

entries.criterionSummary: Alendronic acid should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to impaired renal clearance and accumulation risk (E9) and should not be used in patients with upper GI disease including dysphagia, oesophagitis or peptic ulceration (H8).
contextToCheck: Upper GI disease — dysphagia, oesophagitis, ulcers
Swallowing ability (must remain upright 30 min after dose)
Duration of use and indication (osteoporosis prevention or treatment)
entries.whyItMatters: Oesophageal ulceration and failure to clear drug in renal impairment are serious preventable harms.

entries.criterionSummary: Risedronate should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to impaired renal clearance (E9) and should not be used in patients with upper GI disease including dysphagia, oesophagitis or peptic ulceration (H8).
contextToCheck: Upper GI disease — dysphagia, oesophagitis, ulcers
Swallowing ability (must remain upright 30 min after dose)
entries.whyItMatters: Renal impairment and upper GI disease are common in older adults and require careful screening before bisphosphonate prescribing.

entries.criterionSummary: Ibandronic acid should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to impaired renal clearance (E9) and should not be used in patients with upper GI disease including dysphagia, oesophagitis or peptic ulceration (H8).
contextToCheck: Upper GI disease — dysphagia, oesophagitis, ulcers
Swallowing ability (monthly or IV formulation options)
entries.whyItMatters: Oral ibandronate carries similar upper GI risks to other bisphosphonates; renal function must be checked before and during treatment.

entries.criterionSummary: Zoledronic acid should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to risk of acute kidney injury and accumulation; its IV route bypasses upper GI risks (E9).
contextToCheck: eGFR — contraindicated if <30, use with caution if 30–35
Hydration status at time of infusion
Calcium and vitamin D correction before administration
Indication — oncology versus osteoporosis dosing differs
entries.whyItMatters: IV administration bypasses GI concerns but acute post-infusion nephrotoxicity is a well-recognised risk in frail older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Sildenafil should be avoided in patients with severe heart failure with hypotension, or in those taking concurrent nitrate therapy, due to profound hypotension risk (B14).
contextToCheck: Heart failure severity and baseline blood pressure
Indication — erectile dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension?
entries.whyItMatters: The combination with nitrates is an absolute contraindication that can cause life-threatening hypotension.

entries.criterionSummary: Tadalafil should be avoided in patients with severe heart failure with hypotension, or in those taking concurrent nitrate therapy, due to profound hypotension risk (B14).
contextToCheck: Heart failure severity and baseline blood pressure
Other antihypertensives (alpha-blockers used for BPH — amplify hypotension)
Indication — erectile dysfunction, BPH or pulmonary hypertension?
entries.whyItMatters: Tadalafil has a long half-life (17.5 hours), meaning nitrate interaction risk persists for an extended period.

entries.criterionSummary: Vardenafil should be avoided in patients with severe heart failure with hypotension, or in those taking concurrent nitrate therapy, due to profound hypotension risk (B14).
contextToCheck: Heart failure severity and baseline blood pressure
QT-prolonging potential — caution with other QT drugs
entries.whyItMatters: Combination with nitrates is absolutely contraindicated; even without nitrates, severe heart failure with hypotension makes PDE5 inhibitors unsafe.

entries.criterionSummary: Spironolactone combined with other potassium-conserving drugs without electrolyte monitoring carries hyperkalaemia risk (B13) and should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to hyperkalaemia accumulation (E7).
contextToCheck: Serum potassium — monitor with any K-conserving combination
Concurrent ACE-I, ARB, or potassium supplements
entries.whyItMatters: Hyperkalaemia from spironolactone can be life-threatening, particularly in renal impairment or with ACE-I/ARB combinations.

entries.criterionSummary: Eplerenone combined with other potassium-conserving drugs without electrolyte monitoring carries hyperkalaemia risk (B13) and should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to hyperkalaemia accumulation (E7).
contextToCheck: Serum potassium — monitor with any K-conserving combination
Concurrent ACE-I, ARB, or potassium supplements
entries.whyItMatters: Life-threatening hyperkalaemia is the dominant risk; renal function and electrolyte monitoring are mandatory.

entries.criterionSummary: Isosorbide mononitrate should be reviewed in patients with recurrent falls and persistent postural hypotension, as vasodilation may worsen haemodynamic instability (K3).
contextToCheck: Indication — is antianginal therapy still appropriate?
entries.whyItMatters: Nitrate-induced vasodilation can precipitate symptomatic postural hypotension and falls, especially in frail older adults on multiple antihypertensives.

entries.criterionSummary: Isosorbide dinitrate should be reviewed in patients with recurrent falls and persistent postural hypotension, as vasodilation may worsen haemodynamic instability (K3).
contextToCheck: Indication — is antianginal therapy still appropriate?
entries.whyItMatters: Nitrate-induced hypotension contributes to falls risk, requiring indication review in patients with postural instability.

entries.criterionSummary: Glyceryl trinitrate should be reviewed in patients with recurrent falls and persistent postural hypotension, as acute vasodilation may precipitate syncope and falls (K3).
contextToCheck: Patient education: sit or lie down after SL dose
entries.whyItMatters: Acute GTN-induced vasodilation is a common precipitant of syncope in older adults; patient positioning after use is essential.

entries.criterionSummary: Hyoscine butylbromide is flagged in delirium or dementia due to its anticholinergic burden (D14) and in patients with chronic constipation as it worsens bowel motility (F3).
contextToCheck: Indication — is an alternative antispasmodic available?
entries.whyItMatters: Anticholinergic burden from hyoscine compounds in cognitively impaired or constipated older adults can precipitate delirium or bowel obstruction.

entries.criterionSummary: Hyoscine hydrobromide is flagged in delirium or dementia due to its significant anticholinergic burden including CNS penetration (D14) and in patients with chronic constipation (F3).
contextToCheck: Indication — travel sickness or end-of-life secretion management?
Duration of use (patch formulation provides continuous exposure)
entries.whyItMatters: Hyoscine hydrobromide crosses the blood-brain barrier and can directly precipitate delirium and worsened cognition.

entries.criterionSummary: Nitrofurantoin should be avoided if eGFR <45 ml/min/1.73 m², as reduced renal clearance impairs urinary drug concentration and increases systemic toxicity including pulmonary and peripheral neuropathy risk (E8).
contextToCheck: History of pulmonary reaction to nitrofurantoin
Duration — long-term prophylaxis increases toxicity risk
entries.whyItMatters: Below eGFR 45 the drug fails to achieve therapeutic urinary concentrations and systemic adverse effects, including pulmonary fibrosis, accumulate.

entries.criterionSummary: Colchicine should be avoided if eGFR <10 due to toxicity accumulation (E5) and should not be used long-term for chronic gout when a xanthine oxidase inhibitor is indicated (H6).
contextToCheck: Long-term use for gout — is allopurinol or febuxostat indicated?
Concurrent drugs that raise colchicine levels (e.g. clarithromycin, ciclosporin)
entries.whyItMatters: Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index; accumulation in renal impairment causes severe GI toxicity, myopathy and bone marrow suppression.

entries.criterionSummary: Theophylline should not be used as monotherapy for COPD when better-tolerated alternatives with superior evidence (LABAs, LAMAs) are available (G1).
contextToCheck: Is this genuinely monotherapy for COPD?
Drug interactions — numerous (e.g. quinolones, macrolides raise levels)
entries.whyItMatters: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index with significant toxicity (arrhythmias, seizures) and is no longer recommended as first-line COPD therapy.

entries.criterionSummary: Methotrexate should be avoided if eGFR <30 due to impaired renal clearance leading to accumulation and severe toxicity including pancytopenia and mucositis (E10).
contextToCheck: Monitoring bloods — FBC, LFTs, renal function (mandatory regular monitoring)
entries.whyItMatters: Methotrexate toxicity in renal impairment is life-threatening; regular monitoring and dose adjustment are mandatory.

entries.criterionSummary: Lithium has QT-prolonging potential and should be reviewed in patients with known QTc prolongation or concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (B15); it also requires regular monitoring for toxicity given its narrow therapeutic index.
contextToCheck: Serum lithium level (narrow therapeutic index 0.4–1.0 mmol/L in older adults)
Renal function — toxicity accumulates as eGFR falls
Hydration and sodium intake — dehydration raises levels
entries.whyItMatters: Lithium toxicity is life-threatening and its risk is amplified in older adults by age-related renal decline, dehydration and drug interactions.

entries.criterionSummary: Levothyroxine should be reviewed in patients with subclinical hypothyroidism where TSH is below 10 mU/L and free T4 is normal, as treatment benefit is unproven and over-replacement increases AF and bone loss risk (J9).
contextToCheck: TSH level — is it above 10 mU/L?
Free T4 — is it within normal range?
Whether diagnosis is subclinical or overt hypothyroidism
entries.whyItMatters: Over-treating subclinical hypothyroidism increases the risk of atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis and fracture in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Desmopressin should not be used for urinary incontinence or frequency in older adults due to significant risk of hyponatraemia (J10).
contextToCheck: Indication — is this for nocturia, enuresis or urinary frequency?
Concurrent diuretics or drugs causing SIADH
entries.whyItMatters: Desmopressin causes hyponatraemia in older adults through water retention, risking confusion, seizures and falls.

entries.criterionSummary: Megestrol acetate should not be routinely used to stimulate appetite in older adults as evidence of benefit is limited and it carries significant thromboembolic and adrenal suppression risks (F8).
contextToCheck: Indication — has multidisciplinary nutritional assessment been done?
Whether evidence-based nutritional interventions have been tried
entries.whyItMatters: Appetite stimulation with megestrol provides marginal benefit while risking deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and adrenal insufficiency.

entries.criterionSummary: Perphenazine carries antimuscarinic burden and is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH (D4), delirium or dementia (D14), as a first-line phenothiazine for psychosis or BPSD given EPS profile (D21), and as a falls risk (K2).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH
entries.whyItMatters: Phenothiazines as a class carry significant EPS, anticholinergic and sedative risks in older adults with dementia.

entries.criterionSummary: Pipotiazine as a depot phenothiazine is flagged in lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH (D4), delirium or dementia (D14), as a first-line phenothiazine for psychosis or BPSD (D21), and as a falls risk (K2).
contextToCheck: Lower urinary tract symptoms or BPH
Depot formulation — frequency review and cannot rapidly dose-adjust
entries.whyItMatters: Depot formulation means adverse effects from high anticholinergic and EPS burden cannot be rapidly reversed if problems arise.

entries.criterionSummary: Piracetam lacks evidence of cognitive benefit in dementia and should not be used for this indication in older adults (D20).
contextToCheck: Indication — is this prescribed for dementia or cognitive decline?
Whether evidence-based dementia treatments have been optimised
entries.whyItMatters: Prescribing agents without evidence of benefit in dementia adds medication burden without clinical gain.

entries.criterionSummary: Modafinil lacks evidence of cognitive benefit in dementia and should not be used for this indication in older adults (D20).
contextToCheck: Indication — is this prescribed for dementia-related cognitive impairment or excessive daytime sleepiness?
Cardiovascular effects (raised BP and heart rate)
entries.whyItMatters: Cardiovascular stimulant effects and lack of dementia evidence make modafinil inappropriate for cognitive enhancement in older adults.

entries.criterionSummary: Ginkgo biloba lacks robust evidence of cognitive benefit in dementia and should not be used for this indication (D20).
contextToCheck: Indication — is this being used for cognitive decline or dementia?
Concurrent anticoagulants or antiplatelets (ginkgo inhibits platelet aggregation)
Whether it is being counted in the medication list for interactions
entries.whyItMatters: Ginkgo biloba has antiplatelet effects that increase bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulants, despite lacking evidence for dementia benefit.

entries.criterionSummary: Ramipril should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs such as spironolactone or potassium supplements (B13).
contextToCheck: Concurrent potassium-conserving drugs (aldosterone antagonists, potassium-sparing diuretics, supplements)
eGFR trend — check after initiation or dose change
entries.whyItMatters: Hyperkalaemia from ACE inhibitor use in combination with potassium-conserving agents can precipitate life-threatening arrhythmia.

entries.criterionSummary: Lisinopril should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
entries.whyItMatters: Unopposed hyperkalaemia from ACE inhibitor plus potassium-conserving drug combinations carries arrhythmia risk.

entries.criterionSummary: Perindopril should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
entries.whyItMatters: Hyperkalaemia risk must be actively monitored in any ACE inhibitor combined with aldosterone antagonists or potassium supplements.

entries.criterionSummary: Enalapril should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
entries.whyItMatters: Electrolyte disturbance from ACE inhibitor combinations can be life-threatening if unmonitored.

entries.criterionSummary: Losartan should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
entries.whyItMatters: ARBs carry identical hyperkalaemia risk to ACE inhibitors, particularly in combination with aldosterone antagonists.

entries.criterionSummary: Candesartan should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
contextToCheck: Heart failure indication (candesartan has strong HFrEF evidence)
entries.whyItMatters: Combination with aldosterone antagonists and renal impairment are common co-factors amplifying ARB-associated hyperkalaemia.

entries.criterionSummary: Irbesartan should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
entries.whyItMatters: Unmonitored hyperkalaemia in ARB-plus-potassium-conserving regimens can precipitate fatal arrhythmia.

entries.criterionSummary: Valsartan should be withheld in patients with hyperkalaemia (serum K >5.5 mmol/L, B12) and requires electrolyte monitoring when combined with other potassium-conserving drugs (B13).
entries.whyItMatters: Regular electrolyte monitoring is essential in any ARB regimen involving potassium-conserving co-medications.

entries.criterionSummary: Atenolol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia <50 bpm or significant heart block (B4), as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension where superior alternatives exist (B5), and in combination with AChE inhibitors due to additive bradycardia (D18).
contextToCheck: Indication — is this genuinely first-line for hypertension?
Peripheral vascular disease or cold extremities
entries.whyItMatters: Atenolol's use as sole antihypertensive is not guideline-recommended and its combination with rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers risks complete heart block.

entries.criterionSummary: Bisoprolol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia <50 bpm or significant heart block (B4), as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension (B5), and in combination with AChE inhibitors due to additive bradycardia (D18).
contextToCheck: Indication — heart failure, AF rate control, or hypertension?
Asthma or COPD (bisoprolol is cardioselective but caution needed)
entries.whyItMatters: Bisoprolol is commonly used in heart failure but combination with calcium-channel blockers or AChE inhibitors risks bradyarrhythmia.

entries.criterionSummary: Propranolol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia or heart block (B4), as antihypertensive monotherapy (B5), as a non-selective beta-blocker in diabetes with frequent hypoglycaemia (J3), and combined with AChE inhibitors (D18).
contextToCheck: Asthma or obstructive airways disease (non-selective — contraindicated)
entries.whyItMatters: As a non-selective beta-blocker, propranolol masks hypoglycaemia symptoms and is contraindicated in asthma; it also carries the class-wide heart block risk with calcium-channel blockers.

entries.criterionSummary: Carvedilol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia or heart block (B4), and in combination with AChE inhibitors due to additive bradycardia (D18).
entries.whyItMatters: Carvedilol's additional alpha-blockade amplifies orthostatic hypotension risk compared to cardioselective beta-blockers.

entries.criterionSummary: Metoprolol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia or heart block (B4), as antihypertensive monotherapy (B5), and in combination with AChE inhibitors (D18).
contextToCheck: Indication — AF rate control, heart failure or hypertension?
Asthma (cardioselective but caution at higher doses)
entries.whyItMatters: Rate-limiting drug combinations with metoprolol can precipitate complete heart block, particularly in older adults with pre-existing conduction disease.

entries.criterionSummary: Nebivolol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem due to heart block risk (B3), in bradycardia or heart block (B4), as antihypertensive monotherapy (B5), and in combination with AChE inhibitors (D18).
contextToCheck: Indication — heart failure in older adults or hypertension?
entries.whyItMatters: Despite vasodilatory properties, nebivolol carries the class-wide bradyarrhythmia risk with concurrent rate-limiting agents.

entries.criterionSummary: Sotalol is flagged in combination with verapamil or diltiazem (B3), in bradycardia or heart block (B4), as antihypertensive monotherapy (B5), as a QT-prolonging agent (B15), and in combination with AChE inhibitors (D18).
contextToCheck: Renal function (sotalol renally cleared — QT risk rises with eGFR reduction)
entries.whyItMatters: Sotalol's class III antiarrhythmic properties prolong the QT interval; in renal impairment, accumulation markedly increases the risk of torsades de pointes.
